definition: MLOps (machine learning operations) is the set of practices and tools that keep a model working reliably after it leaves the notebook — versioning data and code, tracking experiments, automating deployment, and monitoring behavior once it's live, instead of treating 'it worked once' as the finish line.

The ML lifecycle is the repeating loop a model goes through for as long as it's in use: train it, validate it, deploy it, monitor how it behaves on real traffic, and retrain it when things drift — then start the loop again, rather than treating the project as done after one deployment.

Reproducibility is being able to get the same result from an ML experiment again later, which takes more than just keeping the same code — the exact training data, the exact library/environment versions, and the random seed all have to match too, or the numbers can quietly shift.

A random seed is a starting number that makes a program's 'random' choices (like shuffling data or initializing a model's weights) come out the same way every time it runs, which is why fixing the seed is one of the requirements for reproducing a training result exactly.

Data versioning means snapshotting a training dataset the same way version control snapshots code, so you can go back and retrieve the exact rows a model was actually trained on months later — without it, a dataset can quietly change underneath you and old results become impossible to reproduce.

DVC (Data Version Control) is a popular open-source tool that versions large datasets and model files alongside your git repository, so a git commit can point to the exact dataset snapshot that produced a given result.

A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training starts — like the learning rate or batch size — as opposed to a value the model learns on its own from data; experiment trackers log these so you know exactly what produced each result.

MLflow is a widely used open-source platform for managing the ML lifecycle, with a Tracking component (logging runs), a Model Registry, and packaging tools — most teams encounter it first through MLflow Tracking.

MLflow Tracking is the part of MLflow that logs each training attempt as a 'run' — recording its parameters, metrics, and output files — and gives you a web UI to browse and compare runs afterward, for example by calling mlflow.log_param() and mlflow.log_metric() inside a training script.

In experiment tracking, a run is one recorded attempt at training a model — a single execution with its own logged parameters, metrics, and artifacts — which is what lets you line up dozens of attempts side by side and see which one actually worked best.

In experiment tracking, an artifact is any output file a training run saves and logs alongside its parameters and metrics — a trained model file, a plot, or a report — so that specific run's full output is still there to look at later.

Weights & Biases (usually shortened to W&B) is a hosted experiment-tracking tool similar to MLflow, best known for two extras: sweeps for automated hyperparameter search and shareable web dashboards for comparing runs.

A sweep is W&B's automated hyperparameter search: instead of you manually trying a learning rate, then another, then another, you tell it what to vary and it launches a whole batch of training runs on its own, then shows you which combination scored best.

A model registry is a central catalog of trained model versions, each with metadata and a lifecycle stage attached, so a team can find, promote, or roll back a specific model version instead of hunting through saved files on someone's laptop.

A lifecycle stage is a label on a model version in a registry — commonly Staging (being tested), Production (serving real traffic), or Archived (retired) — that tells everyone at a glance what that version is currently used for.

A feature store is a shared system that computes and stores the input features models use, split into an offline store (for training) and an online store (for live predictions), so both places compute the same feature the same way.
The offline store is the half of a feature store built for training: it holds large batches of historical feature values, optimized for scanning lots of data rather than answering instantly.
The online store is the half of a feature store built for live predictions: it holds the latest feature values and is optimized to answer a single lookup in milliseconds.

Training-serving skew is when the features a model saw during training don't quite match the features it sees in production — often because two separate pieces of code compute the same feature slightly differently — which quietly hurts accuracy without any obvious error.

Feast is a popular open-source feature store: real software that implements the offline/online store split, letting a team define features once in code and serve them consistently to both training jobs and live models.

A FeatureView is Feast's way of grouping a set of related features that come from the same underlying data source, so they can be defined, versioned, and served together as one unit instead of one at a time.

A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is the shape most pipeline tools use to describe a workflow: steps connected by arrows showing what depends on what, with no loops allowed — once you finish step C you can never route back into step A.

Kubeflow Pipelines is an orchestration tool purpose-built for ML that runs on Kubernetes, where each pipeline step (called a component) executes inside its own container so different steps can use different dependencies and run on different machines.
In Kubeflow Pipelines, a component is one packaged, reusable step of a pipeline (like 'preprocess' or 'train'), bundled with its own code and dependencies into a container.

Apache Airflow is a widely used open-source tool for scheduling and running pipelines defined as DAGs — it's general-purpose (not built specifically for ML) but gets used heavily to orchestrate training and data pipelines.
Prefect is an open-source pipeline orchestrator, like Airflow, but built around writing flows as plain Python functions that can branch and change at runtime instead of a fixed DAG defined upfront.
A quality gate is a check built into a CI pipeline that can block a merge or a promotion if something doesn't meet a bar — in ML, that includes checks on the data and the model, not just the code.

Data validation is the practice of automatically checking incoming or training data against expected rules — like a schema, value ranges, or a missing-value limit — before it's trusted for training or serving.
Continuous training (CT) is the practice of automatically retraining a model on a regular basis, so it doesn't quietly go stale as the world (and the data) keeps changing.

Cron is the classic scheduling syntax (five fields for minute, hour, day, month, and weekday) used to fire a job at a fixed time — the same syntax whether it's retraining a model or backing up a database.

Champion/challenger is a pattern where a newly trained model (the challenger) is compared against the model currently running in production (the champion), and only takes over if it actually performs better.

A model artifact is the packaged output of training: the trained weights plus metadata like the framework and version used to produce them — the thing that actually gets deployed, as opposed to the training code that created it.
Inference is the act of running a trained model on new input to get a prediction — as opposed to training, which is the process that produced the model in the first place.

Inference code is the small amount of code that loads a trained model's weights and runs a prediction on new input — it travels together with the weights in a packaged model artifact, since the weights alone can't do anything.

ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is a shared, open file format for trained models, letting a model trained in one framework — say PyTorch — be exported and then served by tools built for a completely different framework.

Batch inference means running a trained model over a large pile of stored data all at once, on a schedule, with no live user waiting on an immediate answer — like scoring every order from last night in one nightly job.

Online inference (also called real-time inference) means answering one prediction request at a time through a live API call, with a response expected back in milliseconds — like a fraud check that runs the moment you hit checkout.

Streaming inference means running a model continuously against a live, ongoing feed of events as they arrive — a middle ground between batch's fixed schedule and online's one-request-at-a-time pattern.

A model server is a dedicated piece of software that loads a trained model and exposes it over a network API (REST or gRPC), handling things like versioning and concurrent requests, so you don't have to hand-write a server around your model.
TensorFlow Serving is Google's dedicated open-source server for deploying trained TensorFlow models, exposing them over gRPC or REST and handling model version swaps without downtime.
TorchServe is the PyTorch community's equivalent of TensorFlow Serving: a dedicated server built specifically for deploying and serving models trained in PyTorch.

NVIDIA Triton Inference Server is a model-serving tool that can host models from multiple frameworks at once — TensorFlow, PyTorch, ONNX, and more — side by side on the same GPU-optimized server, instead of locking you into serving just one framework's models.

Sending a new model version to only a small slice of live traffic first — say 5% — while the rest keeps using the old, proven version. If the canary looks healthy you gradually ramp it up to 100%; if not, you've only exposed a handful of users to the problem.

Running a new model on real, live traffic in parallel with production, but throwing away its output instead of showing it to anyone. You get a true read on how it would perform on real requests with zero risk to actual users, since only the old model's answers ever go out the door.
Automatically reverting traffic back to a model's last known-good version when live metrics — like error rate — cross a bad threshold, instead of waiting for a person to notice and act.

Watching the overall shape of what a model is predicting over time — for example, the split between classes it outputs, or the range of numbers it returns — so a silent shift (like a spam filter suddenly flagging 90% of email) shows up even when latency and error rates still look fine.

The probability a model attaches to its own prediction, showing how sure it is. A rising share of low-confidence predictions is often an earlier warning sign of trouble than accuracy itself, since accuracy needs the real outcome to arrive first.

The actual, correct outcome for a prediction once it's known — like whether a loan was really repaid, or whether an email really was spam. It's what you compare a model's past predictions against to measure real accuracy, and it often arrives well after the prediction itself.

A shift in the statistical shape of a model's input data over time — for example, a loan model trained on applicants averaging age 35 suddenly seeing mostly 22-year-olds. The model hasn't changed, but the world feeding it data has.

A shift in the relationship between inputs and the correct output, even when the inputs themselves look the same. Classic example: buying patterns that reliably predicted future purchases before a pandemic stopped meaning the same thing once behavior changed — the same input no longer implies the same correct answer.

A check on the data itself rather than on your code's logic — for example, confirming an 'age' column never holds a negative number, or that a required field is never empty — run before that data ever reaches a model.

A model behavioral test that changes something the model shouldn't care about — like swapping a loan applicant's name — and expects the exact same output. If the prediction changes anyway, that's a sign of hidden, unwanted bias.

A model behavioral test that checks a prediction moves in the expected direction when an input changes in a meaningful way — for example, a higher square footage should predictably push a predicted house price up, not down.

A short, standardized document that ships alongside a model, covering its intended use, its training data, its known limitations, and its measured performance — like a nutrition label, but for a model, so anyone using it knows its limits upfront.

A required human sign-off step before a model is promoted to production, usually reserved for higher-stakes models — like one deciding loan approvals — the same instinct as a code review, applied to a model release instead of a code change.

The overall set of practices — documentation, approval workflows, and fairness checks — that make sure a model is reviewed and understood before it ships, instead of only being investigated after something goes wrong.

A comparison of a model's performance across different subgroups — for example, checking a hiring model approves resumes at similar rates across genders — because a model can look accurate overall while quietly performing worse for one group.

Tracking changes to an LLM prompt over time the same way you'd track changes to code or a registered model — so you know exactly which prompt text produced which behavior, and can roll back a bad edit just as easily as rolling back a bad model version.

Using one LLM to score the quality of another LLM's output, instead of comparing it against one fixed expected answer — useful because the same prompt can produce a differently-worded (but equally correct) answer every time it runs.

Tracking how much each LLM call actually costs, since usage is billed by tokens in and out — a subtle prompt change or a longer conversation history can quietly multiply your bill even while accuracy stays perfectly fine.
